transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
A death row inmate in Tennessee who survived a failed execution last night is now hospitalized
in critical condition.
Christa Pike's attorneys say their client was afraid she'd suffer complications with
lethal injections because of a blood disorder that made it difficult to get needles into
her veins.
On NPR's Here and Now Today, Catherine Sweeney with Member Station WPLN describes a level
of confusion surrounding Pike's attempted execution.
It took a really long time for them to establish IV access.
Because there's a curtain over the window that whole time, we don't know what went wrong.
They pushed this enormous amount of sedative that is designed to kill somebody by a pretty
broad margin.
They ended up running it twice and she was still alive.
She was talking at points where she should have been appearing comatose.
She was lifting her head up and looking around.
WPLN's Catherine Sweeney reporting, "Governor Bill Lee has paused all executions in his state
pending a third-party review, but he says he plans to uphold jury sentences."
The people of Tennessee have determined that the death penalty is the appropriate penalty
for the most heinous crimes in this state.
The people of Tennessee make that decision and my job is to make sure to them that those
sentences are carried out.
Pike was 20 when she was convicted of the 1995 murder of a classmate.
She's now 50 and has been fighting her death sentence on the grounds that her history of
childhood sexual abuse and mental illness were not fully considered at the time of sentencing.
President Trump is visiting Texas and Oklahoma today while Vice President J.D. Vance visits
Florida in a bid to energize Republican bases in the deep red states ahead of the midterm
elections in less than five weeks.
He does so with national polls suggesting low public approval ratings for high energy
prices inflation and the U.S. war with Iran.
The Congressional Budget Office has directly linked the war to elevated inflation, which
recently prompted the Fed to hike interest rates for the first time in more than three
years.
Federal prosecutors have filed more charges against the man accused of planting two bombs
in Washington, D.C. on the eve of the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot and P.E.R.'s Ryan Lucas
has the latest on the case against Brian Cole Jr.
Cole was arrested in December after a nearly five-year FBI investigation.
Prosecutors say he built and planted two pipe bombs near the Republican and Democratic Party
headquarters in Washington the night before President Trump supporters angry about his
2020 election loss stormed the U.S. Capitol.
Neither of the bombs went off.
Cole has pleaded not guilty.
Now, prosecutors have filed a new indictment, adding four additional charges, bringing the
total number of counts Cole is facing to eight.
He is currently scheduled to go on trial in February.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR.
Mortgage rates are at their highest level in almost three years, according to Freddie
Mac, the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is now almost 7.3 percent.
NPR's Stephen Besaha reports that follows a sharp rise in bond yields.
Mortgage interest rates often go up with the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, and that
yield has been floating around a more than two decade high.
Mortgage rates are up a quarter of a percent from last week.
John Diamond is an economist at Rice University, and he says the high cost of borrowing is
having a bad lock-in effect on the economy.
People are staying put, that's going to slow down consumption growth, but hopefully that
will eventually lead to lower inflation.
The Federal Reserve will consider raising interest rates again later this month to fight
inflation.
Stephen Besaha, NPR News.
A report published today shows that glaciers in Switzerland lost more than five percent
of their volume this year.
More from NPR's Rob Schmitz.
The report by the Swiss Academy of Sciences is based on data collected by the Glacier
Monitoring Network at the public university, ETH Zurich.
It found that following a year with exceptionally little winter snow and a summer of record-breaking
temperatures, glacier thickness decreased by an average of 8 to 13 feet across monitored
glaciers.
Over the past five years, Switzerland, home to the most glaciers in the European Alps,
has lost nearly 20 percent of its total glacier volume.
Several of the country's smaller glaciers have now completely and permanently disappeared,
while remaining glaciers continue to retreat at an accelerated pace.
Rob Schmitz, NPR News.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News, in Washington.
Stay tuned for the following announcements and messages from our sponsors.

topics.text: Death row inmate Christa Pike survives failed execution in Tennessee, hospitalized in critical condition
Governor Bill Lee pauses all executions in Tennessee pending third-party review of execution procedures
President Trump visits Texas and Oklahoma while VP Vance visits Florida ahead of midterm elections
Congressional Budget Office links U.S. war with Iran to elevated inflation and recent Fed rate hike
Federal prosecutors file additional charges against Brian Cole Jr., accused of planting D.C. bombs January 5, 2021
Mortgage rates reach highest level in almost three years at 7.3 percent, following Treasury yield increases
Swiss glaciers lose more than five percent of volume in one year due to record temperatures
Switzerland lost nearly twenty percent of total glacier volume over past five years in Alpine region
